data_description: The recordings come from a biometrics study, not a gesture-vocabulary study: Guna, Humar and Pogacnik built an implicit user-identification system in which a person is recognised from the way they pick up or handle a Wiimote, aimed at low-stakes login (e.g. multimedia services).

data_description: A computer-vision shape-classification study. Thakoor & Gao needed pairs of *similar* shape classes to test a discriminative HMM shape classifier, and built two purpose-made databases; the second was vehicle silhouettes segmented out of outdoor traffic video by a motion-based object extractor.
benchmark_task: Classify a univariate length-577 series (an unrolled vehicle outline) into one of four body types.
source_publication: Thakoor & Gao, "Shape Classifier based on Generalized Probabilistic Descent Method with Hidden Markov Descriptor", ICCV 2005, Sec. 7.2 (read in full, CiteSeerX copy): "In the second experiment, we classified the vehicles shapes extracted from traffic videos using the motion information... The vehicles were classified into one of the four class: sedan, pickup, minivan or SUV." Same section: "Videos were captured at resolution of 320 x 240. As object extraction approach used does not deal with shadows, the extracted car shapes are distorted in the bottom half due to shadow. 30 samples for each class were extracted from the video." The companion database page (biomecis.uta.edu/shape_data.htm) states the shapes are stored as "Cartesian coordinates of each point on the perimeter of the shape".

data_description: EPANET simulation of chlorine concentration at every node of a drinking-water network over 15 simulated days, produced by Li et al. (KDD 2009) to evaluate a missing-value imputation method; no domain classification target was ever defined for it.
benchmark_task: Classify a univariate length-166 series (a cross-section of chlorine concentration across the 166 network nodes) into three undocumented classes.
source_publication: Li, McCann, Pollard, Faloutsos, "DynaMMo - Mining and Summarization of Coevolving Sequences with Missing Values", KDD 2009, Sec. 4.1.2 Datasets (read) - "Chlorine Dataset (Chlorine) - The Chlorine dataset (see sample in Figure 6(a)) was produced by EPANET 2 that models the hydraulic and water quality behavior of water distribution piping systems. ... The data set consists of 166 nodes (pipe junctions) and measurement of the Chlorine concentration level at all these nodes during 15 days (one measurement for every 5 minutes, a total of 4310 time ticks). Since the water demand pattern during the 15 days follows a clear global periodic pattern (daily cycle, dominating residential demand pattern), EPANET would correctly reflect the pattern in the Chlorine concentration with a few exceptions and slight time shifts." The archive page attributes the data to Lei Li's CMU PhD thesis; both links it gives (cs.cmu.edu/~leili/pubs/leili-thesis.pdf and .../li-kdd09.pdf) are dead (HTTP 404), and the thesis itself was not reached - the KDD'09 paper above is the same data described by the same authors.
stakeholder_and_use: water utilities / EPANET modellers care about residual chlorine across a network; but nobody outside the archive poses the shipped 3-class problem, so the benchmark task has no identified user.
source_target: None; EPANET simulation built to test missing-value imputation
original_task_reasoning: The source (Li et al., KDD 2009) simulated the data with EPANET to evaluate a missing-value imputation and summarization method; it posed no classification target.
data_origin_note: The shipped series runs over the 166 network nodes at one time tick (the source matrix transposed); the archive text describes it as 15 days of 5-minute measurements.
benchmark_target: Three undocumented classes
task_construction_reasoning: Benchmark target: Three undocumented classes. Source target or purpose: None; EPANET simulation built to test missing-value imputation. Label attached by: Curators. Mechanism 'task replacement': the curators imposed three classes, of undocumented meaning, on simulation output that had no labels.
split_provenance: Archive default split; who built it and by what rule is not documented [R]
split_reasoning: The audit describes cases taken at nearby times in one simulated system. A training case and test case can therefore describe almost the same system conditions. The result tests more cases from that simulation. It does not show whether the model works on a new simulation run; similarity between cases would need a separate check.
assumptions_and_inferences: New case assumed for the split verdict: New simulation runs. Split evidence: train and test are cross-sections at adjacent time ticks of one 15-day simulation run; adjacent ticks are near-duplicates [R]. Label: three classes imposed by curation over EPANET output; the source study had no labels and the classes are undocumented [R]. Series length 166 equals the EPANET node count, so the shipped index is network node, not time (the archive text describes 15 days of 5-minute measurements) [R]; the three classes were imposed by the curators with undocumented meaning [R].
open_questions: The source posed no classification target; what the three archive classes mean, how they were assigned, and how the simulation ticks were allocated to train and test are undocumented in every source consulted.

stakeholder_and_use: cardiologists / non-invasive infarct localisation (electrocardiographic imaging)
source_target: Infarct extent and location
original_task_reasoning: The source study posed its own prediction task, which the archive did not keep as the label.

assumptions_and_inferences: New case assumed for the split verdict: New recording occasions. Split evidence: the archive defines the four classes as four people, so each person is on both sides [S]; that a person's series share one session and are electrodes on the same torso at the same moment [R]. open_questions: The 2007 challenge identification is our inference; the archive page says only 'one of the Computers in Cardiology challenges'.

data_description: These series come from the UK government-sponsored household electricity monitoring study known as "Powering the Nation" (the DECC/Defra/Energy Saving Trust Household Electricity Survey).
benchmark_task: Classify a 720-point daily consumption profile as a desktop or a laptop computer.
source_publication: UK Household Electricity Survey (DECC, Defra and the Energy Saving Trust, 2010-2011); Intertek Report R66141, "Household Electricity Survey: A study of domestic electrical product usage", final report issue 4. Household counts differ: the archive page, the thesis and Intertek (p. 24) give 251 households, Report 5 (p. 4) and gov.uk give 250; the 26 year-long households were sampled every 10 minutes except from late November 2010 to February 2011, when they recorded every 2 minutes (Intertek p. 64). Curated into TSC datasets by Lines & Bagnall (UEA): J. Lines, PhD thesis, UEA, 2015, Sec. 3.2.2 and Table 3.3 ("We provide five new classification problems that focus on domestic appliance classification from electricity consumption"); introduced in Lines & Bagnall, "Ensembles of elastic distance measures for time series classification", SIAM SDM 2014 (not read: no full text found).
stakeholder_and_use: UK energy policy (the survey); the curators' stated aim was to extract more from smart-meter data by "classifying appliances according to their electricity usage profiles". The derived task (naming a device from its own metered daily profile) is appliance recognition, not disaggregation of a whole-house load.
source_target: Household electricity monitoring for energy policy (Household Electricity Survey); each metered channel is annotated with its appliance, but the survey posed no classification task
original_task_reasoning: The survey's installing electricians annotated each monitored product with its appliance ("selected from a dropdown list"), so under policy L3 we count appliance-type recognition as the source's own task although the survey trained no classifier; the classification problem was posed on those annotations by the curators (Lines & Bagnall, SDM 2014; Lines 2015 thesis). Each input is an appliance trace metered on its own, so the task is appliance recognition, not whole-house disaggregation.
benchmark_target: which computing device produced the day's consumption trace (desktop vs laptop)
task_construction_reasoning: The benchmark label is the survey's appliance annotation of the metered channel (which computing device produced the day's consumption trace (desktop vs laptop)); label origin: source task, by the convention that a collectors' annotation of the quantity a deployed model would predict counts as the source task.
split_provenance: Archive default split, made by the curators (Lines & Bagnall), who say these datasets were "split in a certain manner to avoid introducing bias" from one device appearing in both train and test [S]; the rule used is not stated and the files carry no household or device identifiers [R]
split_reasoning: The source measured each physical appliance over many days. We do not know whether all days from an appliance or household were kept in one set. If the same appliance appears in both sets, the model may recognise its usual pattern. That would be a narrower test than recognising appliance types in new homes.
family_relation: five appliance-group tasks cut from the UK Household Electricity Survey (ElectricDevices comes from a different study, the Visual Energy Trial); whether they share households or appliances is not documented
assumptions_and_inferences: New case assumed for the split verdict: New appliances or households. Split evidence: each series is one day cut from a month (or, for some households, a year) of metering, so one appliance can supply many series [R]; which households, appliances and days entered the dataset is not documented. The curators say the split was made to avoid device bias, but give no rule, and the files carry no device identifiers, so device- or household-disjointness is neither documented nor refuted and sharing is not counted as leakage [R]. An appliance-recognition model meeting unseen appliances is the deployment case [I].
open_questions: Appliance-type recognition is counted as the source task by convention (the survey annotated the channels but posed no classification task); a stricter reading files it as metadata. Appliance/household sharing inferred from the survey design but not documented, so Unclear rather than Concern.

benchmark_task: Classify a normalized length-300 single-axis wrist-accelerometer series as one of twelve cricket umpire signals.
source_publication: Ko, West, Venkatesh, Kumar, "Online Context Recognition in Multisensor Systems using Dynamic Time Warping", ISSNIP 2005 (DOI 10.1109/ISSNIP.2005.1595593). Not read: the paper is closed access (Unpaywall reports oa_status "closed"; the archive's own second_link is a dead IEEE Xplore login URL, and the Semantic Scholar "open access" copy at dro.deakin.edu.au returns an empty file). Layer 1 above therefore rests on the archive description page, the UCR briefing document and the UEA archive paper's description of the multivariate version.
stakeholder_and_use: sports-video annotation and automatic scoring systems; more generally the source authors' interest was online context recognition from wearable multisensor streams
source_target: which of twelve cricket umpire signals was performed
original_task_reasoning: The source study posed a classification target that a stakeholder outside the paper needed.
benchmark_target: which of twelve cricket umpire signals was performed
task_construction_reasoning: The benchmark label is the target the source study posed (which of twelve cricket umpire signals was performed); label origin: source task.
split_provenance: Archive default split; who built it and by what rule is not documented [R]
split_reasoning: The data contain repeated gestures, but the files do not say which person produced each case. We cannot check whether all gestures from a person were kept in one set. A test gesture might come from someone already represented in training. Performance on people the model has never seen is therefore not established.
multivariate_source_note: The source recorded acceleration from wrist-worn accelerometers; the UCR release keeps a single channel of it. Five of the six original channels are dropped (both wrists x three axes reduced to one axis), so gestures that differ mainly in the other arm's motion or in the plane of movement become harder or impossible to separate. Amplitude is removed by the donors' normalization, and the length normalization to 300 removes gesture duration. The problem the source posed is multivariate, and its place is the multivariate archive, where it already exists as Cricket.
family_relation: X, Y and Z are the same recordings projected onto three axes; UEA Cricket is the multivariate version
assumptions_and_inferences: New case assumed for the split verdict: New people. Split evidence: 390/390 split not documented as subject-disjoint; no subject id in the files [R].

data_description: Land-cover / crop-type mapping from satellite image time series. Tan, Webb & Petitjean (SDM 2017, Sec. on SITS classification) describe the source data: "In this work, we used 46 geometrically and radiometrically corrected images taken by FORMOSAT-2 satellite...
benchmark_task: Classify a length-46 per-pixel reflectance profile into one of 24 land-cover classes.
source_publication: Tan, Webb & Petitjean, "Indexing and classifying gigabytes of time series under time warping", SDM 2017 (read; the archive's data_source_link bit.ly/SDM2017 resolves to the figshare project for this paper). The related TempCNN paper (Pelletier, Webb & Petitjean, arXiv:1811.10166, Sec. 3.1-3.2) describes the same imagery: "The satellite dataset is composed of 46 Formosat-2 images acquired at 8 meter spatial resolution during the year 2006", with reference data from "farmer's declaration from 2006... ground field campaigns performed during 2006... and a reference map obtained with a semi-automatic procedure" (that paper aggregates to 13 classes rather than 24).
stakeholder_and_use: agricultural and environmental agencies producing land-cover maps (the data were released with permission of CesBIO and the French Space Agency)
source_target: land-cover / crop class of a ground pixel (24 classes)
original_task_reasoning: The source study posed a classification target that a stakeholder outside the paper needed.
benchmark_target: land-cover / crop class of a ground pixel (24 classes)
task_construction_reasoning: The benchmark label is the target the source study posed (land-cover / crop class of a ground pixel (24 classes)); label origin: source task.
leakage_evidence: exact cross-split matches (2753 of 16800 test series)
split_provenance: Tan et al. (2017) release, 7200 train / 16800 test pixels of one scene and season; assignment rule undocumented [R]
split_reasoning: The cases are pixel sequences from one scene and season. Nearby pixels may describe the same field and growing conditions. The value check also finds 2,753 of 16,800 test cases identical to training cases. This makes the test different from evaluating new fields, scenes or seasons.
multivariate_source_note: The source recorded sequence of satellite reflectance observations for one 8 m ground pixel over a growing season; the UCR release keeps a single channel of it. Spatial context around the pixel is dropped (each pixel is treated independently), the multi-band signal is reduced to one channel, and z-normalization removes the absolute reflectance level, which is physically informative for land cover. The temporal axis itself is preserved intact. The problem the source posed is multivariate, and its place is the multivariate archive; no multivariate version of it is in UEA.
assumptions_and_inferences: New case assumed for the split verdict: New fields, scenes or seasons. Split evidence: all pixels come from one 64 km2 scene and one season; neighbouring pixels of one field are near-duplicates and 2753 of 16800 test pixels are identical to training pixels; a land-cover model is deployed on new fields and years [R]+[D].

data_description: There is no external "original problem" here in the sense of a domain study that posed this task. The underlying data are hourly averaged seismic readings from the Northern California Earthquake Data Center (NCEDC), Dec 1967 to 2003, a monitoring archive rather than an experiment.
benchmark_task: Classify a 512-point hourly seismic window as preceding a major event or not.
source_publication: timeseriesclassification.com description page for Earthquakes, which is the curators' own account: "We transform this single time series into a classification problem by first defining a major event as any reading of over 5 on the Rictor scale... Hence we consider a positive case to be one where a major event is not preceded by another major event for at least 512 hours. To construct a negative case, we consider instances where there is a reading below 4... that is preceded by at least 20 readings in the previous 512 hours that are non-zero (to avoid trivial negative cases). None of the cases overlap in time (i.e. we perform a segmentation rather than use a sliding window). Of the 86,066 hourly readings, we produce 368 negative cases and 93 positive." No separate peer-reviewed paper describing this curation was located, nor documentation of exactly which NCEDC quantity was "averaged" per hour.

data_description: UCR's computational entomology group built cheap pseudo-acoustic optical sensors — a laser line pointed at a phototransistor array — that record the light fluctuations caused by an insect's wings occluding the beam as it flies through.

data_description: Calibrated humidity and temperature streams from a wireless sensor-mote deployment (CMU), used by Sun and Faloutsos as an unsupervised testbed for tracking correlations among co-evolving streams; Keogh later cut windows from two streams and used the stream identity as the class.

data_description: Automated classification of variable stars. Sky surveys produce brightness measurements of hundreds of millions of celestial objects, far more than astronomers can inspect; the standing task is to assign each variable star to its physical type from the shape of its light curve.

data_description: Semiconductor manufacturing process control. Plasma-etch tools used to fabricate silicon wafers carry large numbers of in-line sensors; if a tool drifts outside tolerance during any of the 250-plus processing steps, yield and reliability suffer or the wafer is scrapped.
benchmark_task: Classify a length-152 etch-tool sensor trace as a normal or abnormal processing run.
source_publication: Olszewski, "Generalized Feature Extraction for Structural Pattern Recognition in Time-Series Data", PhD thesis, Carnegie Mellon University, CMU-CS-01-108, 2001 (read in full from cs.cmu.edu/~bobski). Sec. 4.3.2, p. 65: "A collection of in-line process-control measurements recorded from various sensors during the processing of silicon wafers for semiconductor fabrication constitute the wafer database; each data set in the wafer database contains the measurements recorded by one sensor during the processing of one wafer by one tool." Same section, p. 66: "The data sets contained in each database were analyzed by appropriate domain experts, and a label of normal or abnormal was assigned to each data set. Of the 1194 data sets in the wafer database, 1067 data sets were identified as normal and 127 data sets were identified as abnormal." On which sensors: p. 66-67, "six parameters have been identified by domain experts as being critical for monitoring purposes: radio frequency forward power, radio frequency reflected power, chamber pressure, 405 nanometer (nm) emission, 520 nanometer (nm) emission, and direct current bias" and p. 69, "Previous experiments have shown that the most accurate classification of wafer data sets can be accomplished using the 405 nm and 520 nm parameters."
stakeholder_and_use: semiconductor fabs running statistical process control on etch tools — catching an out-of-tolerance run early avoids scrapping wafers
source_target: whether the process run recorded by the sensor was normal or abnormal, as judged by a domain expert
original_task_reasoning: The source study posed a classification target that a stakeholder outside the paper needed.
benchmark_target: whether the process run recorded by the sensor was normal or abnormal, as judged by a domain expert
task_construction_reasoning: The benchmark label is the target the source study posed (whether the process run recorded by the sensor was normal or abnormal, as judged by a domain expert); label origin: source task.
split_provenance: Archive default split, 1000 train / 6164 test; not stated in Olszewski's thesis, author and rule undocumented [R]
split_reasoning: The archive ships all six sensor traces of each wafer as separate cases and split them without regard to wafer or run. Matching every shipped series to the raw files shows 690 wafers and 99 of 104 production runs on both sides; every training series has another sensor of its wafer in test. The test therefore does not measure performance on new wafers or runs.
multivariate_source_note: Each wafer was recorded by six in-line sensors. The release ships all six traces as separate univariate series and drops the sensor identity and the wafer and run grouping, so the multivariate structure a process-control system would use is gone. The thesis itself classified single sensors (the 405 nm and 520 nm parameters) and left combining them to future work; no multivariate version is in UEA.
assumptions_and_inferences: New case assumed for the split verdict: New wafers or production runs. data_description: Behavioural genetics in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. Worm locomotion is a standard readout for gene function: mutants move differently from wild type, so quantifying movement is a way to phenotype genes.
benchmark_task: Classify a length-900 first-eigenworm amplitude series (one worm, ~15 minutes of crawling at 1 Hz) into one of five strains. 181 train / 77 test.
source_publication: Brown AE, Yemini EI, Grundy LJ, Jucikas T, Schafer WR, "A dictionary of behavioral motifs reveals clusters of genes affecting Caenorhabditis elegans locomotion", PNAS 110(2):791-796, 2013. Only the abstract was reached (the PNAS full text returned HTTP 403 and PubMed/EuropePMC did not render); the quoted sentence above is from that abstract. The C. elegans behavioural database (http://wormbehavior.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/) is named by the archive page as the source of the traces, and the archive page reproduces the formatting description from Bagnall et al.'s bake-off paper.
stakeholder_and_use: Geneticists and neurobiologists using C. elegans as a model organism, who need high-throughput behavioural phenotyping to link genes to behaviour.
source_target: Unsupervised discovery of behavioural motifs across strains (Brown et al. 2013); no classification target
original_task_reasoning: The source collected the data but posed no classification target: Brown et al. built an unbiased dictionary of behavioural motifs, and the strain of each recorded worm was the experimental factor, not a prediction target.
benchmark_target: worm strain: N2 wild type or one of the mutants goa-1, unc-1, unc-38, unc-63
task_construction_reasoning: Benchmark target: worm strain: N2 wild type or one of the mutants goa-1, unc-1, unc-38, unc-63. Source target or purpose: Unsupervised discovery of behavioural motifs across strains (Brown et al. 2013); no classification target. Label attached by: Curators. Mechanism 'metadata as label': the archive derives the classes from a recording attribute; the strain is known before recording and was the source's experimental factor.
leakage_evidence: exact cross-split matches (10 of 77 test series)
split_provenance: 181 train / 77 test, identical for Worms and WormsTwoClass; rule undocumented [R]
split_reasoning: The original record describes each case as a separate worm recording. However, the value check finds 10 of 77 test cases identical to training cases. We therefore need worm and recording identifiers to resolve the disagreement between that source description and the released values.
multivariate_source_note: The source recorded video of a single worm crawling on an agar plate, tracked at 30 frames per second; the UCR release keeps a single channel of it. Two reductions, both large. (1) Shape: each video frame's full worm outline is collapsed to a single scalar, the amplitude along the first eigenworm - three of the four shape dimensions are discarded, so postures that differ in eigenworms 2-4 are indistinguishable here. The problem the source posed is multivariate, and its place is the multivariate archive, where it already exists as EigenWorms.
family_relation: Worms and WormsTwoClass are the same traces with the same split, mutant strains collapsed in the latter; UEA EigenWorms derives from the same C. elegans behavioural database
assumptions_and_inferences: New case assumed for the split verdict: New worms or recordings. Split evidence: each series is one worm's recording; plate or batch is not shipped [R]. Strain labels used as classes where the source study was unsupervised motif discovery over the same strains; the strain is recording metadata, so the task is counted as constructed [S].
open_questions: The strains were the source's experimental factor, so a strain classifier is a supervised proxy for the phenotyping question the study asked; we count the label as metadata because the source posed no classification target.
